Let the zeros be the consecutive positive integers t,t+1,\ldots,t+K-1. First, any nonzero exponential sum with n distinct positive bases has at most n-1 consecutive zeros: if it vanished at n consecutive integers, the coefficient vector would lie in the kernel of an n\times n Vandermonde matrix, which is nonsingular. Thus K\le n-1.

We show K\ne n-1. Suppose f(t),\ldots,f(t+n-2)=0. Put c_m=a_m m^t. Then
\[
\sum_{m=1}^n c_m m^r=0\qquad(r=0,1,\ldots,n-2).
\]
The one-dimensional kernel of this (n-1)\times n Vandermonde matrix is spanned by
\[
w_m=\frac1{\prod_{j\ne m}(m-j)}.
\]
Since c_1=a_1=1, normalization gives
\[
c_m=(-1)^{m-1}\binom{n-1}{m-1}.
\]
In particular, c_n=\pm1, so
\[
a_n=\frac{c_n}{n^t}=\pm\frac1{n^t},
\]
which is not an integer because n\ge2 and t\ge1. Hence K\le n-2.

For sharpness, define
\[
a_m=(-1)^{m+1}\binom{n-1}{m-1}.
\]
Then a_1=1 and, for 1\le x\le n-2,
\[
f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^j\binom{n-1}{j}(j+1)^x=0,
\]
by the vanishing of the (n-1)-st finite difference of a polynomial of degree at most n-2. Therefore K=n-2 is attainable, and the maximum is \(\boxed{n-2}\).

Using c_1=a_1=1, this yields
\[
c_m=(-1)^{m-1}\binom{n-1}{m-1}.
\]
For m=n, therefore, c_n=\pm1, and so
\[
a_n=c_n n^{-t}=\pm n^{-t},
\]
contrary to the integrality of a_n. Consequently K\le n-2.

\[
a_m=(-1)^{m+1}\binom{n-1}{m-1}\quad(1\le m\le n).

These are integers and a_1=1. For every integer x with 1\le x\le n-2, the polynomial p(j)=(j+1)^x has degree at most n-2, so its (n-1)-st finite difference is zero:
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^j\binom{n-1}{j}(j+1)^x=0.
\]
This sum is f(x). Hence the n-2 consecutive positive integers 1,\ldots,n-2 are zeros. Therefore the maximum possible value is \(\boxed{n-2}\).

We prove that the answer is \(n-2\).

Suppose f vanishes at K consecutive positive integers beginning with t. If K\ge n, then the n equations
\[
f(t+r)=\sum_{m=1}^n(a_m m^t)m^r=0\qquad(0\le r<n)
\]
have a nonsingular Vandermonde coefficient matrix, forcing every a_m m^t, and hence a_m, to be zero. This contradicts a_1=1. Thus K\le n-1.

It remains to exclude K=n-1. In that case, with c_m=a_m m^t,
\[
\sum_{m=1}^n c_m m^r=0\qquad(0\le r\le n-2).
\]
The nullspace is one-dimensional. Its standard Vandermonde null vector is
\[
c_m=\lambda\bigg/\prod_{j\ne m}(m-j).
\]
Because c_1=a_1=1, \(\lambda=(-1)^{n-1}(n-1)!\), and hence
\[
c_m=(-1)^{m-1}\binom{n-1}{m-1}.
\]
Taking m=n gives c_n=\pm1. Therefore \(a_n=\pm n^{-t}\), impossible for an integer a_n since n\ge2 and t>0. Hence K\le n-2.

For equality, choose
\[
a_m=(-1)^{m+1}\binom{n-1}{m-1}.
\]
Then a_1=1. For 1\le x\le n-2,
\[
f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^j\binom{n-1}{j}(j+1)^x=0,
\]
because this is the (n-1)-st finite difference of the polynomial \((j+1)^x\), whose degree is at most n-2. Thus K=n-2 occurs, proving
\[
\boxed{K_{\max}=n-2}.
\]

Let the consecutive zeros be t,t+1,\ldots,t+K-1, where t\ge1.

For K\ge n, write c_m=a_m m^t. The equations f(t+r)=0 for r=0,\ldots,n-1 become
\[
\sum_{m=1}^n c_m m^r=0.
\]
Their coefficient matrix is the Vandermonde matrix on the distinct numbers 1,2,\ldots,n, so it is nonsingular. Hence c_m=0 for every m, contradicting c_1=a_1=1. Therefore K\le n-1.

Assume K=n-1. Then the same equations hold for r=0,\ldots,n-2. The nullspace is one-dimensional, and its entries are proportional to
\[
\frac1{\prod_{j\ne m}(m-j)}.
\]
Normalizing with c_1=1 gives
\[
c_m=(-1)^{m-1}\binom{n-1}{m-1}.
\]
In particular c_n=\pm1. Since c_n=a_n n^t,
\[
a_n=\pm\frac1{n^t},
\]
which contradicts a_n\in\mathbb Z. Thus K\le n-2.

For the lower bound, set
\[
a_m=(-1)^{m+1}\binom{n-1}{m-1}.
\]
These satisfy a_1=1 and are integral. For each x=1,\ldots,n-2, put p(j)=(j+1)^x. Since \deg p=x\le n-2,
\[
0=\Delta^{n-1}p(0)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^{n-1-j}\binom{n-1}{j}(j+1)^x.
\]
Multiplying by \((-1)^{n-1}\) gives f(x)=0. Hence there are n-2 consecutive positive-integer zeros, and the upper bound is attained. Therefore
\[
\boxed{K_{\max}=n-2}.
\]
